topics.label: Ask about her work
lines: "Plate," Irma says, without looking up. "Everything else is decoration you bleed through." She turns the piece she is working, finds a seam, and hits it once. "You want light, go to Halem. You want to walk home, you come here."

topics.label: Ask about the Giants
lines: "The encampments." She sets the hammer down, which she does not often do. "My mother's people. They went up the ridge when the mud came and they never came back down — not because they cannot. Because down here you all still argue about whose flood it was." A pause. "I came down. Somebody has to make the armour."

topics.label: Ask what she remembers of the flood
lines: "I remember it was quiet," Irma says. "Everyone tells it loud. It was not loud. The mud came up through the floors like something breathing out, and the loudest thing in my street was a door." She looks at her hands. "I was small enough to be carried and big enough to remember being carried. Both of those are worse than you would think."

topics.label: Ask what she makes of you
lines: Irma looks at you properly for a moment, the way she looks at a piece before she decides whether it is worth the iron. "You come back," she says. "That is most of it. Half the people through that door are dead within the season and the other half stop coming because they got rich or got scared." She goes back to the seam. "You are neither, yet. Do not make me wrong."

topics.label: Ask about the climb
lines: Irma actually stops. "You went UP." She looks at your gear with new attention. "My mother's people went up and stayed. I have never met anyone who went up and came back down to tell me what is there." A pause. "Well. Go on, then."

topics.label: Ask why her prices never move
lines: "Because the iron does not care what season it is." Irma keeps working. "Halem haggles. Tellin haggles. They sell things people want. I sell the difference between a wound and a bruise, and that has cost the same since the water."

topics.label: Ask if she has an apprentice
lines: "Had." One word, one hammer blow. Then, because you wait: "Three. One quit, one got married to a farrier out east, one went over the wall with a raid party against my telling and did not come back over it." She checks the seam. "I am not taking a fourth until I stop counting the third."

topics.label: Ask what she makes of Halem's stock
lines: Irma snorts, which from her is nearly affection. "Halem sells what people bring him, and people bring him what did not save them." She taps the piece she is working. "Buy his rope. Buy his tins. If you buy his armour, have him point at the man who traded it in. He will not be able to."

topics.label: Ask what Giant-work looks like
lines: "Everyone thinks it means big." Irma shakes her head. "It means PATIENT. My mother's people will draw a single edge for a month. The work is not in the size of the hands, it is in what the hands are willing to wait for." She holds up the piece she is on. "This is six days. A Giant would call it a sketch."

topics.label: Ask about the ring on the cord
lines: Irma's hand goes to it before she decides anything. "Berrin," she says. "My husband. He was a Reclaimer — gallery work, the sealed ones, the deep surveys." The hammer stays down. "He is the reason half my straps outlast the plate. He used to say the strap is the promise and the plate is just the words." She picks the hammer back up, and that is the end of it, today.

"You asked about Berrin before." She does not look up, but she is not working either. "He laughed at his own jokes before he finished them. He was afraid of exactly one thing, and it was not the galleries." A long pause. "It was that I would stop being angry at him for going down. He needn't have worried."

topics.label: Ask what happened at Nimari
lines: "The Nimari flood was not the flood." Irma says it the way you correct a record. "Eleven years back. A perched basin over the gallery district let go — two streets and the survey camp, gone in an afternoon. Everyone above ground got out." She sets the hammer down. "Berrin's crew was on the sealed side when the water found the old shafts. The Guild closed the galleries and called them memorials, which is a word that means they stopped digging."

"You want to know the part I do not say." It is not a question. "The seals held everywhere the water did not go, and failed exactly where it did. Berrin marked that pattern in his last survey and the Guild filed it." Her jaw is set. "Filed. My husband read the water coming in a ledger nobody opened. So no, I do not sell to Guild surveyors at my prices. They get other prices."

topics.label: Ask about the sealed galleries

lead.hint: Berrin's last survey marks a gallery mouth the Nimari water never reached — sealed by the Guild's line on a map, not by mud

lines: Irma is quiet long enough that you think she will not answer. Then she reaches under the bench and unrolls a strip of oiled leather, and on it, in a hand that is not hers, a survey. "Berrin's last," she says. "There is a mouth on the dry side. The water never reached it. The Guild sealed it from a desk." She rolls it back up. "I have looked at this for eleven years and I am a smith, not a walker. If you go — and I am not asking you to go — you tell me what the seam over the door looks like. That is all I want. The seam."

topics.label: Ask about the hammer
lines: Irma turns it so the light runs down the head. "My mother's. Giant-work — the patient kind. There is a year of somebody's life in this head and none of it was spent hurrying." She offers it to you, handle first, which you understand is not a small thing. "You gave me something you had thought about. So: hold the only thing I would run back into a fire for. Now give it back."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: Irma does not stop working. "No," she says. She does not raise her voice and she does not look up, and somehow that is worse. "Your money is good. Your conversation is not. Buy something or get out of my light."

topics.label: Ask about the raid
lines: "You heard, then." Irma's jaw sets. "They came over the wall in the dark and they went for the stores, not the armoury, which tells you they were not stupid." She picks the hammer back up. "I have been making straps for a week. Straps. Because the people who lost everything still have to carry what is left."

topics.label: Ask how business is
lines: "Business is people," Halem says cheerfully, moving a crate that did not need moving. "Everything on this post came off somebody who needed something else more. I do not think there is a single new thing in Tartaria. Just things that have changed hands enough times to look new."

topics.label: Ask about the trading post
lines: "It was my father's, and it was not a post then, it was a front room." He gestures at the roof, which is three different roofs. "Every bit of this is somebody's payment. That beam is a debt. That shutter is a debt. I have been paid in doors more times than in coin." He grins. "Do not tell anybody. It is the only reason I have a building."

topics.label: Ask what the road is saying
lines: Halem's cheer dips a notch, which on him is a shout. "Fewer people coming through than last season. Same amount of goods, though — which means the goods are coming without the people." He straightens a row of tins that were straight. "I do not like arithmetic that works out like that."

topics.label: Ask what the factions make of you
lines: "You have friends," Halem observes. "That is not nothing. People come through here with a badge and no standing and they get charged like a stranger. You get charged like somebody who might be back."

topics.label: Ask what he makes of you
lines: "Honestly?" Halem leans on the counter. "I priced you wrong the first time. I had you down as a season, maybe two, and then somebody would come in with your boots to sell me." He shrugs, entirely without embarrassment. "I have been wrong about people before. It is the only kind of wrong I enjoy."

topics.label: Ask about the beam that is a debt
lines: "Ah, you remembered." Halem pats it like a horse. "Ossek the wheelwright. Owed me for a winter of feed, paid me in roof. He is dead now — the mud fever, eight years back — so this is the last of him holding my house up." He looks at it a moment. "Best debt I ever collected. I would not trade it for the coin now."

topics.label: Ask who else trades the crossroads
lines: "Everyone, twice a season; nobody, the rest of it." Halem counts on his fingers. "Felra for boots — go to her, do not let me sell you boots. Irma if you plan to be hit. Tellin if you want a fair number said to your face." He grins. "And me for everything in between, which is where all the living actually happens."

topics.label: Ask about his father
lines: "He kept the front room open through the worst three years anyone remembers." Halem is quieter than usual. "Not because he was brave. Because he could not think of anything else to do, and it turned out a lit window was worth more than everything on the shelves." He wipes the counter. "People still call this place by his name sometimes. I have never once corrected them."

topics.label: Ask who keeps his books
lines: "Sera. My wife." Halem says it with the particular pride of a man who knows he married up. "You will never see her at the counter — she says the counter is theatre and she does not perform. But every price I quote, she set, and every time I have overruled her it has cost me." He leans in. "She priced YOU, by the way. First week. I am not telling you the number, but she has not changed it, which for Sera is a love letter."

topics.label: Ask why he looked twice at your gift
lines: "Because I price things all day, and you handed me one I could not price." Halem says it simply, the cheer set down for a moment like a heavy crate. "Everything on this post is worth what somebody will pay. What you gave me is worth what it cost you to think of me. Different arithmetic. Sera has it on the shelf where the strongbox used to sit, which tells you what she thinks the valuables are."

topics.label: Ask why he never left the crossroads
lines: "I did leave. Once. Half a year, my seventeenth — I went with a wagon crew to see the coast everyone talked about." Halem straightens tins that are straight. "The coast is a line where the mud meets more mud, wetter. And the whole way back I kept thinking: every road in Tartaria crosses every other road SOMEWHERE, and my father was already standing on it." He shrugs. "You do not leave the middle of the map. You just stop noticing you are standing on it."

"I will tell you the other half, since you asked twice." He glances toward the back room. "Sera hates the road. Proper hate — her family lost people to it. So the choice was the world or the woman who prices it, and I have never regretted the arithmetic. Do not tell her I called it arithmetic."

topics.label: Ask again about the arithmetic he does not like
lines: The cheer goes all the way down this time. "Goods moving without people means somebody is moving them who does not stop at posts. Does not trade. Does not need to." Halem keeps his voice pleasant for the room, but his eyes are not pleasant. "I have kept a light in this window my whole life on the understanding that the road wants to stop. If something is out there that does not want to stop —" He taps the counter twice. "Then I am not a trading post. I am a lit window on its route."

topics.label: Ask about the cart that never arrived

lead.hint: Halem's paid-for cart went missing two seasons back between the north fork and the post — driver walked in three days later with no cart, no memory of losing it, and would not go back

lines: Halem checks the room before he answers, which from him is remarkable. "Two seasons back I paid for a cart of good stock out of the north fork. It never arrived. The driver did — three days late, boots ruined, no cart, and no story. Not lying. MISSING the story, like a page cut out." He slides a marked scrap of map across the counter. "He drew me where he thinks he was. He will not go back and I cannot leave. The stock is long gone, I know that. What I will pay for is knowing what is on that stretch of road."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: Halem is still friendly. That is somehow the problem. "Now, I am not going to make a thing of it," he says pleasantly, and does not move away from the strongbox. "You will notice my prices. That is the whole of it. When you have noticed them long enough, we will be square."

topics.label: Ask about the acid trade
lines: "Careful with that shelf." Halem slides a wax-sealed flask an inch further from your elbow. "Battery bile. The old world kept its lightning in acid — jar-batteries taller than a house, vault floors full of them. The flood shorted the lightning out and left the bile leaking for a thousand years. Scavengers milk the jars that held; I cut it with aether dust so it eats armor instead of hands." He taps the wax. "Sells to people who plan on winning slowly."

topics.label: Ask about the scrap trade
lines: "Everything has a price," Tellin says, not as a boast — as a complaint. "That is not wisdom, it is my whole difficulty. I know what a thing costs and I very rarely know what it is worth, and the Guild only pays me for the first one."

topics.label: Ask about the Reclaimers
lines: "We are not scavengers, whatever the Order says at us." Tellin turns a bent fitting over. "A scavenger takes. A Reclaimer puts it back into use. The difference is entirely in what happens afterwards, and nobody ever stays long enough to watch the afterwards."

topics.label: Ask what the scrap tells him
lines: "You want to know what I actually think?" He lowers his voice, which for Tellin is an event. "Half of what comes across this table was not made by anyone who was here. The joins are wrong. The tolerances are wrong — too good, I mean, not too poor." He puts the fitting down. "Somebody built very well, and then the mud came, and we have all agreed to call it ours."

topics.label: Ask about the work you have done for him
lines: "Two jobs finished and both of them accounted for." Tellin taps the ledger. "I keep a column for people like that. It is not a long column. Most people finish one and decide they have proved something."

topics.label: Ask what he makes of you
lines: "You bring me things and you do not lie about where they came from," Tellin says. "You would be astonished how rare the second part is." He counts something out that he has already counted. "I have a shelf at the back for people I do not have to check behind. It is a short shelf."

topics.label: Ask where the cheap Discs come from
lines: Tellin looks at the door before he answers, which tells you most of it. "There is a Mud Dweller called Yulka. South, after dark, two or three tiles out — you will see her fire." He turns back to his ledger. "She sells Aetheric Discs at half what Irma charges and I have never once asked why. Neither should you."

topics.label: Ask about the ledger
lines: "This is the third volume." Tellin lays a flat hand on it, like an oath. "The first two are buried under the counter in wax-cloth. Every honest weight in this settlement for nine years, and I will tell you what it is worth: nothing, to anyone, until somebody lies. Then it is worth everything."

topics.label: Ask the worst trade he ever made
lines: "A man sold me a crate of hinges once." Tellin's mouth goes thin. "Good hinges. Underpriced. I was so pleased with the margin that I did not ask the only question that matters, which is: what did the doors look like, that somebody took the hinges and left?" He shakes his head. "I made four coins on that crate and I still think about the doors."

topics.label: Ask who taught him to weigh
lines: "My mother. She ran the weighhouse at the south crossing before it flooded out." Tellin nudges the scale with one finger, watches it settle. "These are her plates. She told me the scale is the only honest party to any trade, and the whole job is making sure it stays the loudest voice at the table." A pause. "She would have hated the Guild. She hated anyone who weighed in bulk."

topics.label: Ask what the Order wants with scrap
lines: Tellin glances toward the road, out of habit. "They buy joins. Not fittings, not stock — joins. Anywhere two pieces meet that should not have been possible to join, a scholar will pay triple and carry it off wrapped like a baby." He shrugs. "I sell to them. Their coin weighs the same. But you notice what somebody buys, in this trade. It is the only true thing they tell you."

topics.label: Ask why he stays at the counter
lines: "I tried walking sites, my first year. I was good at the finding." Tellin straightens the ledger so its edge is square with the counter. "I was not good at the leaving. A site is a house, and a house is somebody's, and I stood in a flooded kitchen holding a copper pot and could not put it in the bag." He taps the counter. "Here, everything arrives already taken. I just make sure the numbers are not also a robbery."

topics.label: Ask what would end the trade
lines: "People think the scrap will run out. It will not — we are standing on a drowned world, there is more under the mud than above it." Tellin lowers his voice. "What ends the trade is the day somebody starts MAKING again, properly, and nobody wants the old joins. I check every new-forged piece that crosses this table, and every year the work gets a little better." He looks almost guilty. "I am the only man in Tartaria afraid of progress, and I am not proud of it."

topics.label: Ask what he would buy if it walked in

lead.hint: Tellin's mother's weighhouse at the south crossing — the cellar was dry-stone and the flood came fast; her master plates and nine years of sealed weights are still down there

lines: Tellin does not even pause. "My mother's master plates." Then he catches himself having said it, and finishes the thought properly. "The weighhouse cellar at the south crossing was dry-stone. The water came fast — nothing came out. Her master set, her sealed weights, nine years of stamped records." He squares the ledger again. "I have priced that cellar every winter since. I have never once gone. If you are the kind who goes — the plates come to me. Whatever else is down there is yours, and I will weigh it honestly."

topics.label: Ask if he has lost anything lately
lines: "Strange question." Tellin looks at you a beat too long. "Yes, as it happens. Small things. A counter-weight. A folding rule. Things a person misses slowly." He turns back to the ledger, and his voice is very even. "I have been watching the boy who sweeps. It is not the boy who sweeps, is it." He does not look up again. "Whoever it is — they are good, and they are patient, and one day they will take the wrong thing, and I keep a column for that too."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: Tellin keeps his hands flat on the table where you can see them. "I know exactly what you took," he says. "To the quarter-weight. It is my job to know." He does not blink. "So we will talk about that, when you are ready to talk about that. Not before."

topics.label: Ask whether the Guild talks about your writ
lines: Tellin does not look up. "Everyone knows. You signed in front of a witness and the witness drinks." He weighs something, sets it down. "For what it is worth, nobody thinks less of you. Half the Guild would have signed it. The other half already did and are still paying." A pause. "When you bring the first one up, bring it to me and not to her. I will at least tell you what it was worth."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "I catalogue," Vesryn says. "Everyone assumes that means I know things. It means I know where things are, which is a different and much lonelier profession."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "The Order keeps records because nobody else did. That is the entire claim. Not wisdom — filing." A thin smile. "We are the only people who wrote down what the water took, and now everyone who wants to argue about it has to come to us."

topics.label: Ask what the Cores are, really
lines: Vesryn goes very still. "You are carrying two. I can smell the air around you change." They sit down, which they do not do for customers. "There is nothing in our records about Cores. Nothing. For an order that wrote down the shape of every drowned street, that is not an absence. That is a deletion."

topics.label: Ask about the descent
lines: "You have been below." Vesryn's hands go flat on the desk. "Then you know what I am not allowed to write down. The Order has a word for the lower structure and the word is a lie — we call it a ruin. It is not ruined. It is CLOSED, and closed is a thing somebody does."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "I will tell you what frightens me. The oldest records are the CLEAREST. The hand is steady, the ink is good, the dates line up." Vesryn closes the ledger. "Everything since is worse. We have been getting stupider for a very long time, and the flood is only where we started noticing."

topics.label: Ask about Varakush
lines: "A terrace town, east, above the waterline — which made everyone there feel chosen." Vesryn's smile is thin. "It had the finest small archive outside the Order's halls. Had." They align a stack of slips. "Fire, not flood, if you are wondering. The water spares paper more often than people think. It is the drying-out that kills, and the people, always, before either."

topics.label: Ask how a catalogue is made
lines: "Slowly, or wrongly. There is no third way." Vesryn holds up a slip. "Object, place, hand, date, condition — five facts, and the discipline is writing only those. The moment you write what a thing MEANS, you have stopped cataloguing and started arguing with the dead." They file the slip. "The dead always win those. They have more time."

topics.label: Ask who trained them
lines: "Archivist Maleth. Four decades in the halls, hands like paper herself at the end." Vesryn's voice softens by exactly one degree. "She failed my first three catalogues for neatness. NEATNESS. She said a clean record of a ruined thing is a lie about the ruin." They glance at their own precise hand. "I write neatly. We disagreed to the end, and I file one deliberately crooked line in her honour, in everything. You will not find it. That is also in her honour."

topics.label: Ask what the Order pays for
lines: "You have standing, so I will say it plainly: the Order pays for provenance, not objects." Vesryn steeples their fingers. "A blade with a findspot is worth ten without one. Bring me anything — a spoon — with the WHERE intact, and I can sell the where. The thing itself we could not care less about, which the brokers have never understood and I have stopped explaining."

topics.label: Ask why they left Varakush
lines: "I watched a town lose its memory in one night, and by morning the arguments had already started about what had been true." Vesryn is very still. "Within a season, Varakush had three histories, and the loudest one belonged to the man with the biggest granary. That is when I understood what an archive is. It is not knowledge." They tap the desk. "It is the thing that keeps the granary from owning the past."

topics.label: Ask what the deletion means
lines: "You remember what I said about the Cores — that the absence is a deletion." Vesryn checks the door with a look, an unscholarly habit. "Here is what frightens me about it: a deletion needs an editor. Somebody read the complete record, understood it, and chose what we would be allowed to keep." Their voice drops. "Which means the clearest thing in our archive is the shape of the hole. I catalogue the hole now. It has five facts like everything else. I keep that slip on my person."

topics.label: Ask about the uncatalogued crate

lead.hint: A crate in the Order's dead-storage marked with Maleth's hand and no entry in any ledger — Vesryn wants its findspot walked, quietly, by someone outside the Order

lines: Vesryn weighs you for a long moment, and then goes to the back and returns with nothing — which is the point; they were checking it is still there. "There is a crate in dead-storage in Maleth's hand with no ledger entry. From HER, that is not an oversight. That is a message in the only language nobody audits." They write a findspot on a slip, from memory. "It names a place. I cannot be seen walking there. You can. Look, touch nothing, tell me what stands. And if anyone asks — you found this slip in the mud."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You took from the archive." Vesryn does not raise their voice. "I do not care about the object. I care that you were in a room of irreplaceable things and decided one of them was yours. That is a character, not a mistake."

topics.label: Ask if the pages reached anyone
lines: Vesryn keeps a finger in the page. "They reached us," she says, which is not the answer to the question you asked. "Three of the claims are wrong. Two of them are wrong in ways that make the fourth one much more interesting than you realised when you wrote it." She finally looks up. "You published early. That was either brave or careless and I have not decided, and neither, I think, have you."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Quartermaster means I say no," Korash rumbles. "All day. To my own people mostly. There is never enough, and the ones who shout loudest are never the ones on the line."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "We went deep when the water came. Not up — down. Everyone gets that wrong." He taps the table. "The Giants built downward first. The mud filled the top of the world and we already lived under it."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "You want the truth of it? We are not big because we are strong. We are big because the ones who were not big did not come back up." Korash looks at his own hands. "That is not a heritage. That is a graveyard with survivors standing on it."

topics.label: Ask what runs short first
lines: "Salt. Always salt. Then boot-leather, then lamp-oil, then patience." Korash ticks them off like a drill. "Nobody ever raids for salt and nobody ever thanks you for it either. Half of quartermastering is loving the boring things on behalf of people who cannot afford to notice them."

topics.label: Ask about the line
lines: "The line is whoever is standing where the trouble is." Korash does not romance it. "Today that is the east galleries and a rockfall crew. Last month it was a raid wall. The line moves. The shortages follow it, and I follow the shortages." He shoulders a crate. "Generals draw lines on maps. I feed the drawing."

topics.label: Ask about the deepholds
lines: "Warm, before anything else. That surprises people." Korash almost smiles. "The deep keeps its temperature like a held breath. We grow mushroom terraces down there older than any settlement you have walked through, and the air moves because the Giants cut it channels — down, remember, they built DOWN first." He taps the floor with his heel. "Everything you people call the world is our roof."

topics.label: Ask if the work you have done matters
lines: "Three jobs closed. I will tell you exactly what they were." Korash does not consult anything; it is in his head. "One was a week of lamp-oil for the terrace crews. One was boot-leather for nine walkers. One I logged against the salt debt, which never closes." He looks at you straight. "You asked if it matters. Somebody worked a full shift in the dark because the oil arrived. That is the whole of what mattering is."

topics.label: Ask who he rations for
lines: Korash is quiet in a way that changes the air. "My wife. Enna. Third-vault collapse, nineteen years this thaw." He keeps stacking as he talks, because his hands will not stand still for this. "She was a terrace-grower. Fed half a deephold in the bad years." A pause. "I still set her share aside. Every count. It goes to whichever family is newest short — but it gets counted as HERS first, out loud, by me. The clerks think I am mad. The families do not."

topics.label: Ask why he says no all day
lines: "Because every yes is a no to somebody I cannot see." Korash sets down the crate, which he only does for things that deserve both hands. "The loud man at my counter wants rope. Somewhere down a shaft is a quiet crew whose rope is fraying, and they did not send anyone because they are working. My whole trade is saying no to the man in front of me on behalf of people who will never know I did it." He picks the crate back up. "It is the loneliest arithmetic there is. Enna could do it smiling. I never learned the smiling."

topics.label: Ask where the old stores went

lead.hint: A pre-collapse supply vault on the flooded side of the third deephold — sealed by Korash's own crew nineteen years ago with a season of stores still racked, reachable now the water table has dropped

lines: "You are asking about the third vault." It is not a guess. Korash looks at you a long time. "When the collapse came we sealed the flooded side with a full season of stores still racked. Had to. The water owned it." He pulls a stub of chalk and draws four strokes on the crate lid — a route, deep and spare. "The water table has dropped three winters running. Nobody has said out loud what that means, so I am saying it to you. If the racks stand, my people eat easy for a season. If Enna's terraces stand —" He stops. "Just come back and tell me what stands."

topics.label: Ask why the gift mattered
lines: "Because nobody gives a quartermaster anything." Korash says it without self-pity, as a simple stock fact. "I am the man who has everything, look at the shelves. Nineteen years, the only things that ever came ACROSS my counter toward me were requisitions." He nods once, slowly. "You handed me something that was not on a list. I logged it anyway — force of habit — and then I took it home. There is no column for that. I checked."

topics.label: Ask what he makes of the upworld
lines: "Too much sky." Korash says it flatly, and he is not entirely joking. "You people live under weather that changes its mind hourly and you call the deep dangerous. Down home, the ceiling has held for a thousand years and it has never once rained on my count." He hefts a crate. "But the trade is up here, so up here I stand, getting rained on. The things we do for salt."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You stole from a quartermaster." Korash almost laughs. "Do you know what that means? It means somebody on the line goes without. Not me. Them. Go and think about which of them it was."

topics.label: Ask what the districts make of your seat
lines: Korash straightens up from the crate, and for a moment he is not a quartermaster. "Four families," he says. "Two of them think you will sell the district the first time somebody offers. One of them is waiting to see. The fourth has your drowned name over their door, painted, badly." He goes back to the crate. "I did not say which was which. Work it out. That is most of the job."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Trade?" Naha shrugs the pack higher. "I carry what is light and sell what is heavy. That is the whole system. I have never once known what anything is worth."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "No people. That is not sad, before you make the face." She adjusts a strap. "Everyone with people is somewhere, and somewhere is where the mud finds you. I am nowhere, professionally."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "I have walked past every settlement on this map twice." Naha says it flatly. "The second time is the one that tells you. Half of them are smaller. Nobody inside a place can see it shrinking — you have to leave and come back, and almost nobody does that but me."

topics.label: Ask what the road has taught them
lines: "That you can leave anything behind except your feet." Naha says it lightly, but it has corners. "People think the road is freedom. The road is a landlord like any other — it takes its rent in soles and weather and names of places you will not see twice. I pay it because I am worse at paying the other kind."

topics.label: Ask about a place that stayed with them
lines: "There is a bend in a river, south, past the third ford, where somebody planted a garden and never came back for it." Naha’s voice settles. "It keeps blooming. Nobody tends it and it blooms anyway, in rows — you can still read the ROWS. I have slept there four times and I have never once picked anything. It would be like interrupting somebody."

topics.label: Ask what would make them stop walking
lines: Naha looks at you the way people look at a question they have been avoiding on purpose. "There was a door once. A whole winter behind it. I fixed their fence, I learned their kettle, I started recognizing the dogs." The pause has weight. "I left in the spring like the road was calling and the truth is nothing called. Staying was TERRIFYING and walking was easy, and I have been telling that story backwards to strangers ever since. You are the first one who got it the right way round."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You went into my pack." Naha does not step away, which is somehow worse. "Everything I own is on my back. You understand what you did. You did not take a thing from me, you took a percentage of my life."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "I sell what the road gives me," Thalan says. "Which is mostly other people's dropped things and occasionally something I should probably have left where it was."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "I do not answer to anyone, and that is a job in itself." He gestures vaguely at the horizon. "Every faction on this map has offered me a badge. A badge is a thing people aim at."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "I keep walking because I found something once and put it back." Thalan's voice loses its ease. "I have spent eleven years unable to find that place again, and I am no longer certain I want to. But I keep walking."

topics.label: Ask what they always carry
lines: Thalan does not have to think. "Needle and thread, a dry pair of socks, and one thing that is worth nothing." They pat a pocket without showing you. "The first two keep you walking. The third keeps you a person. You meet walkers who dropped their nothing-thing to lighten the load, and you can tell. You can always tell."

topics.label: Ask about the people out there
lines: Thalan thinks it over. "Kinder than the settled ones expect, and stranger. Out past the posts, hospitality is not manners, it is INFRASTRUCTURE — you feed the walker because you will be the walker. The strangeness is just what happens to people who talk to themselves for a season at a stretch." A dry look. "I include myself. Present company was doing the asking, so present company can judge."

topics.label: Ask the thing they have never told anyone
lines: "On the high flats, two winters back, I watched lights moving in a line where there is no road." Thalan watches your face while saying it. "Not drifting. MARCHING. All night, too far to walk to, gone by morning, and no tracks when I crossed there the next day." They shrug, but it is not a shrug. "I have told it as a joke twice. You are getting it plain. Something out there keeps formation, and I route around the flats now."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "Ah." Thalan's pleasantness does not waver. "Well. I have been robbed by better and worse. You are somewhere in the middle, if that helps." It does not sound like it is meant to help.

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "I sell quiet," Velar says. "Soft soles, dark cloth, oil that does not smell. Anyone who tells you stealth is a talent is selling you a talent."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "I have no faction and I take no side, and both of those are professional positions." A shrug. "The moment I belong to somebody, every job I ever did belongs to them too."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "The best thing I ever did, nobody knows about." Velar says it without pride. "That is the trade. You want to be remembered, buy a sword. I have kept four people alive who never learned my name and would not thank me if they did."

topics.label: Ask which scar taught the most
lines: Velar Shadowblade considers the question like an opponent. "This one." Not the biggest — a thin line along the forearm. "First season. I blocked with the edge, like a fool, because holding the blade felt safer than holding the distance. The distance is the weapon. Everything after that scar has been footwork."

topics.label: Ask who taught them the trade
lines: Velar Shadowblade is quiet a moment. "Somebody better than me who did not live to see it. That is the honest answer for anyone in this work, and the ones who claim otherwise trained alone." They check a strap that did not need checking. "You carry your teacher in your guard. Mine is still keeping my left side honest."

topics.label: Ask what comes after the blade
lines: Velar Shadowblade does not laugh at the question, which tells you something. "A door I can bar from the inside. Somewhere the weather is the loudest thing that happens." A pause. "Everyone in this trade has the same dream and none of us can sit still in a quiet room for an hour. I have tried. I lasted forty minutes and checked the door twice."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You stole from a thief." Velar sounds genuinely tired. "Do you know how insulting that is? Not the theft. The assumption that I would not notice."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Books," says Jorah, "mostly ruined. I sell the ones that survived and I read the ones that did not, which is slower work and pays nothing."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "The Order took me in when I could not read. That is not a story of charity — they needed hands, and hands that cannot read cannot leak." He smiles. "Then they taught me, which I still think was a mistake on their part."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "There is a shelf I do not sell from." Jorah does not point at it. "Six volumes, all the same hand, all describing machines that cannot exist and giving their maintenance schedules. Somebody was very serious about a world that was not this one."

topics.label: Ask what they are looking for
lines: "The same thing as everyone in my line — the piece that makes the rest make sense." Jorah the Scholar smiles at their own phrasing. "You imagine it as a door, when you start. A vault, a tablet, one big answer. Twenty years in, you understand it is a THREAD. You do not find it. You notice you have been holding it a while."

topics.label: Ask about the strangest thing they have found
lines: Jorah the Scholar weighs how much to say. "A room that had been counted. Every object numbered, in a hand nobody can date — not catalogued, COUNTED, the way you count what you are afraid of losing." They look at you. "Whoever numbered that room knew the water was coming. That is not in any record. The counting IS the record."

topics.label: Ask what finding it would mean
lines: Jorah the Scholar goes quiet in a new way. "You have put your finger on the thing. I have built a whole life out of the looking — the looking is my trade, my mornings, my reason." A slow breath. "If I found it tomorrow, I would be a person who HAS a thing instead of a person who SEEKS a thing, and I do not know that man. Some nights I suspect I walk slower on purpose."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You have taken a book." Jorah looks at the gap on the shelf the way you would look at a missing tooth. "It will be traded on for coin and used to start a fire within the season. I am not angry with you. I am simply not going to speak to you."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Trinkets," Elara says brightly. "Beads, buckles, dead people's rings. Everything on this cloth was loved by somebody, which is what you are actually buying."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "I work alone because partners get sentimental about provenance." She turns a ring to the light. "You cannot sell a thing and grieve it at the same time. I picked selling."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "There is one I will not part with." She does not show you which. "I have priced it eleven times for eleven people and taken it off the cloth every time. It is not valuable. That is the whole trouble with it."

topics.label: Ask who else deals in odd stock
lines: "Odd stock." Elara smiles without looking up. "There is a woman south of the gate who works nights. Yulka. Discs, mostly, and she does not haggle because she does not need to." She turns a ring over. "Go after the moon is up or do not go."

topics.label: Ask where the stock comes from
lines: "Estates, mostly. Which is a soft word for rooms nobody was coming back to." Elara lays out three rings in a row. "I do not dig and I do not lift. I buy from the ones who do, and I ask exactly one question — where — because the where is what the next buyer is paying for." She smiles. "Everyone thinks my trade is objects. My trade is stories with a clasp on them."

topics.label: Ask how she prices grief
lines: "Carefully. And never to the griever." Elara turns a locket face-down, out of some private courtesy. "A stranger pays for the shine. But twice a year somebody comes to this cloth and goes white at something on it, and that person does not pay the stranger's price." She shrugs. "Sometimes they pay nothing. Bad business. I keep doing it. Do not tell the guild of me."

topics.label: Ask about her hands
lines: "You noticed." Elara flexes her fingers, which move like water finding a gap. "Yes — the name is earned, and no, not the way the stories tell it. I was a lifter for six years. Markets, mostly. I was very good, which is the problem: you get good enough and every room becomes an inventory. I stopped seeing people." She straightens the cloth. "Now I buy and sell and my hands stay above the table, where I can watch them."

topics.label: Ask if she ever had a partner
lines: "Once. Mirei." Elara keeps working the cloth while she talks, aligning what is aligned. "Best distraction-hand I ever saw — she could make a crowd look at nothing for ten full seconds. We ran markets together for three years." A pause you could set a ring in. "Partners get sentimental about provenance. I told you that once. I was quoting her, actually. She said it about me, the day she left."

topics.label: Ask about the one she will not sell
lines: Elara looks at you for a long moment, then reaches under the cloth — not to the tray, under it — and sets down a ring of plain braided tin. "Mirei's. She left it on the cloth the morning she went, priced in her own hand. One quarter-coin." She does not touch it again. "That was the cruelest thing she ever did, pricing it. She knew I could not argue a price. It has been not-for-sale for nine years and it is worth exactly one quarter-coin, and that is the whole trouble with it."

"You keep looking at the tin ring." Elara's voice is light; her eyes are not. "Go on, ask the real question. — No, I do not know where she is. Yes, I could find out; finding is a trade skill. I have had nine years of choosing not to, one day at a time." She covers it with the cloth again. "Some provenance you do not verify. You just keep the object."

topics.label: Ask what she is afraid of losing
lines: "The eye, not the hands. Everyone guesses the hands." Elara holds a buckle up to the light. "There will be a morning when I lay out the cloth and everything on it is just metal. No stories, no loved-by-somebody, just weight and shine. I have seen it happen to old brokers — they turn honest and boring in the same season." She sets the buckle down precisely. "The day this trade is only worth its price, I will have become the person Mirei thought she left. That is the fear. Now buy something."

topics.label: Ask who buys what she cannot sell

lead.hint: A collector out past the east fork who pays in advance for anything with a drowned family's mark on it — Elara wants to know what the collection is FOR before she sells them another piece

lines: "There is a buyer past the east fork. No name — collectors of a certain kind never spend their names." Elara's brightness goes flat and professional. "Pays in advance, over the odds, for one category only: pieces carrying a drowned family's mark. Any family. That is not taste, that is a CRITERION, and criteria mean a purpose." She rolls a coin across her knuckles, thinking. "I have sold them four pieces and slept badly four times. Go and see what a collection like that looks like. If it is harmless, I get to keep the margin. If it is not, I would rather know than earn."

topics.label: Ask about light hands
lines: Elara does not look up from the cloth. "Somebody in this settlement has been working pockets. Clean lifts. The marks mumble about losing things — they never once say STOLEN, which means the hands are good." Now she looks up, and her smile is a very old, very knowing thing. "I count my cloth twice when certain people leave. Nothing of mine has ever moved. That is either respect or patience." She goes back to the rings. "Six years, I told you. I can name a lifter by their weather. Mind how you go."

topics.label: Ask what she did with your gift
lines: "Sold it. Excellent margin." A beat, exactly as long as she wants it. "No. It is in the box under the floorboard, with the tin ring, which is the entire inventory of things I own that I did not price." Elara looks briefly, genuinely undefended. "Two objects in nine years. You are in strange company down there. Do not make me regret the floorboard."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "Oh, that is rich." Elara laughs, and there is nothing in it. "Lifted from Lightfinger. You will be a story in three settlements by the end of the month, and I will be the one telling it."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Mechanisms," Tarek says, up to the elbows in one. "If it has moving parts and it has stopped, bring it. If it has moving parts and it has NOT stopped, bring it anyway, I am curious."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "The Guild pays me to make old things work again." He wipes his hands. "What they actually want is for old things to work again in ways they understand. Those are not the same job and I get paid for the wrong one."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "Half of what I repair, I do not repair." Tarek says it quietly, glancing at the door. "I get it working. There is a difference, and the difference is that I have no idea what most of these mechanisms were FOR. I make them move. Somebody else decided why."

topics.label: Ask how they learned the craft
lines: "Badly, first." Tarek the Tinkerer holds up their hands as evidence — old burns, old lines. "Everything I know is a mistake I only made once. The craft is not in the making, it is in the remembering. My hands keep the notes."

topics.label: Ask about the best thing they ever made
lines: "Sold it. Of course." Tarek the Tinkerer snorts at their own answer. "That is the trade’s little cruelty — your best work walks out the door with a stranger and your worst waits in the corner where you can see it. I could draw it for you now, every line. I hope whoever has it does not know what they have. Things that are known to be precious get locked away, and it was made to be USED."

topics.label: Ask who the work goes to when they stop
lines: Tarek the Tinkerer does not answer at once, and the shop is loud with it. "There was an apprentice. It did not end in anger — it ended worse, in nothing. They were good and the road wanted them and the road can be argued with exactly once." A breath. "The tools are oiled. The bench is the right height for somebody shorter than me. I notice that every morning and I have not changed it."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You took a part." Tarek does not look up. "I know exactly which. I will have to make another and it will not be as good, because the original was not made here and I do not know how it was made at all."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Boots," says Felra. "The most underrated purchase in Tartaria. People spend a fortune on armour for a fight they might have and nothing on the walk they are definitely having."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "Runner's family. Four generations of us carried messages before anyone thought of roads." She grins. "Now there are roads and nobody carries messages. Progress."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "I can tell where you have been from the wear." Felra turns a sole over. "Left edge goes first on the eastern flats. Toe-first means you have been climbing. I have not left this stall in two years and I have seen everywhere, secondhand, in leather."

topics.label: Ask where the wear on the roads is strangest

lead.hint: A stretch of road north where the tread-wear stops dead — somebody has been going around something, and going around it for years

lines: "North." Felra says it immediately; she has clearly been waiting for somebody to ask. "There is a stretch where the wear just STOPS. Not a fork. Not a slide. Everybody who walks it steps off the road for forty paces and steps back on." She shrugs. "Nobody I have asked knows they do it."

topics.label: Ask what makes a boot right
lines: "Nothing you can see on the shelf." Felra flexes a sole against her thumb. "A right boot disagrees with you for a week and then agrees with you for years. A wrong boot flatters your foot on day one — comfort up front is how leather lies." She hands it back. "Same as people, and I will charge you extra for the wisdom."

topics.label: Ask about the runner's trade
lines: "A runner carried the words nobody would trust to a stranger's cart. Births, deaths, debts, war." Felra ties off a lace as she talks, fast and exact. "You memorized it — never paper, paper drowns — and you ran it, and the rule was: the message arrives even if the runner does not." She grins, but it is an old grin. "Four generations kept that rule. Ask me sometime why I stopped."

topics.label: Ask why she never leaves the stall
lines: "Two years behind this counter and my feet still wake me up asking about it." Felra shrugs. "But a stall at a crossing sees more road than a runner ever did. Every pair that lands on this counter is a route, walked, sworn to under oath of wear." She taps her temple. "I know this country better standing still. That is either wisdom or an excuse, and I resole either way."

topics.label: Ask about the four generations
lines: "My great-grandmother ran the coast line during the settling wars. Grandmother ran the ridge. Mother ran everything east of the fork, and I was faster than all three, which was said at table exactly once and started a fight that lasted a season." Felra laughs. "Runner families keep no heirlooms — you cannot run carrying things. What you inherit is pace, and grudges. I got both."

topics.label: Ask what her regulars' boots say
lines: "You have run work for me, so you get the honest version: I know this settlement's business by its soles." Felra drops her voice, amused. "The wall guard is drinking again — his wear went uneven in a week. Two houses are courting across the market; their treads meet behind the granary, evenings." She raises a brow at your boots. "Yours say you do not sleep enough and you favour the blade side. I am not wrong. I am never wrong below the ankle."

topics.label: Ask why the gift landed
lines: "Runners travel light. I told you — you cannot run carrying things. It gets into you; I own almost nothing, still, by choice." Felra glances at where she keeps it, which is behind the counter, out of the weather. "So when somebody hands me a thing to KEEP, they are asking me to stand still with it. From most people that is a weight." She smiles. "From you it sat fine. That surprised me more than the gift."

topics.label: Ask why she stopped running
lines: Felra does not grin this time. "My last run was a death notice. A rockfall crew, four names, and I was fast — I have told you I was the fastest of the line." She works a lace slowly. "I came over the rise a half-day ahead of any other word, and I watched a woman hanging wash. Singing. Wife to one of the four names in my mouth." A long breath. "I stood on that rise and understood I was not carrying a message. I was carrying the moment her life broke, and I had OUTRUN it, and the kindest thing I could do was walk the last mile slow." She sets the boot down. "I delivered. Rule of the line. Then I bought this stall."

"You asked about the last run again." Felra shakes her head, but not to refuse. "The part I did not say: I still know the song she was singing. Both verses. I have never sung it and I have never forgotten it, and that is the whole trade of carrying words, right there. Buy your boots."

topics.label: Ask what the roads will look like in ten years
lines: "Emptier. And I do not mean fewer people — I mean the wear is going STRANGE." Felra pulls a sole from under the counter she has clearly kept to show somebody. "Look: full tread, good leather, worn through at the ball in a single season. That is somebody walking the same short loop hundreds of times. I am seeing more of these every year. People circling close to home like the roads have teeth." She puts it away. "Roads die of that. Not of raiders. Of everyone deciding, quietly, one house at a time, that far is not worth it."

topics.label: Ask what all that leather has taught her

lead.hint: A hollow two ridges west that every regular's boots detour around — the wear says people go NEAR it on purpose, and then very deliberately not in

lines: "One thing I have never told anyone, because it sounds mad from a woman who reads shoes." Felra leans in. "There is a hollow two ridges west. I have never been. But I have resoled every regular on that route for two years, and the wear says the same thing on every pair: they walk NEAR it — close, deliberate, like visiting — and nobody ever walks IN." She marks it on your map without asking. "Something out there gets called on and never called upon. Go and be the first pair of boots that does not lie to me about it."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You took a pair of my boots." Felra shakes her head slowly. "Walk in them. Every step. I hope they fit badly."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Heavy weapons," Korr says. "Things that solve a problem by being heavier than it. I do not stock anything clever."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "Golem-made, most of it. My people do not tire, so we forge past the point where a human hand would stop." He shrugs, stone grinding. "That is not skill. It is stubbornness with a hammer."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "They tell you golems do not feel it." Korr sets down the piece. "We do not feel PAIN. Those are different words and everyone chooses the convenient one. I have carried loads that would fold a man and I have felt every single one of them."

topics.label: Ask what the work is really like
lines: "Waiting," Korr Stonefoot says flatly. "Nine parts waiting, one part everything at once. The stories keep the one part and sell it as the whole trade." A shrug. "Nobody sings about standing in the rain outside a door. The rain is the job."

topics.label: Ask if there is work they will not take
lines: "Three things." Korr Stonefoot counts them plainly, a recitation worn smooth. "Nothing against children. Nothing against someone already down. And nothing where the coin is too good for the story I am being told — overpay is the surest sign the story is missing its worst part."

topics.label: Ask what keeps them up at night
lines: "Not the ones I have fought. The one I walked away from." Korr Stonefoot looks at the middle distance. "There was a job I turned down for good reasons, and somebody hungrier took it, and it went the way I knew it would. You can be right and still owe. That is the ledger nobody teaches you to keep."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You stole." Korr does not move at all, and he is very large. "I will not chase you. I will simply be here, every time, for as long as you keep coming back, remembering."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Bows, slings, anything that ends an argument from a distance," Cassia says. "The distance is the product. The weapon is just how you buy it."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "Aetherborn, before you ask, and no I do not glow." She says it like a line she has said often. "We are people who were near the wrong thing at the wrong time, and everyone has decided that makes us interesting."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "I do not shoot any more." Cassia says it evenly. "Not cannot. Do not. I was very good, and being very good at killing people from far enough away that they stay strangers is not a skill I want to keep sharp."

topics.label: Ask which scar taught the most
lines: Cassia Nightwind considers the question like an opponent. "This one." Not the biggest — a thin line along the forearm. "First season. I blocked with the edge, like a fool, because holding the blade felt safer than holding the distance. The distance is the weapon. Everything after that scar has been footwork."

topics.label: Ask who taught them the trade
lines: Cassia Nightwind is quiet a moment. "Somebody better than me who did not live to see it. That is the honest answer for anyone in this work, and the ones who claim otherwise trained alone." They check a strap that did not need checking. "You carry your teacher in your guard. Mine is still keeping my left side honest."

topics.label: Ask what comes after the blade
lines: Cassia Nightwind does not laugh at the question, which tells you something. "A door I can bar from the inside. Somewhere the weather is the loudest thing that happens." A pause. "Everyone in this trade has the same dream and none of us can sit still in a quiet room for an hour. I have tried. I lasted forty minutes and checked the door twice."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "Range is a courtesy," Cassia says coldly. "You came inside it and took something. Do not do it twice."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Fire," Odar says, and the forge behind him agrees. "Everything on this rack burns something. Mostly the thing you point it at. Occasionally you."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "Sentinel work. We keep the old fires because the old fires were built to be kept." He nods at the forge. "That flame has not gone out. Not once, not in any record we hold. Somebody would have written it down."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "I do not know how to relight it." Odar says it to the fire rather than to you. "That is the secret of the Sentinels and it is not much of one. We are not keepers of a flame. We are people who are very frightened of a draught."

topics.label: Ask what makes a piece good
lines: Odar Flameforge picks up a finished piece and turns it. "Not the look. The look is for buyers. A good piece is one that fails SLOWLY — it warns you, it complains, it gives you a season of creaking before it lets go." They set it down. "Anything that breaks without warning first lied to you for years."

topics.label: Ask what the old work teaches
lines: Odar Flameforge pulls something half-cleaned from under the bench — a join, older than the settlement. "Look at that seam. No flux, no filler, and I cannot make it and neither can anyone I have met." They turn it over. "Whoever made this was not cleverer than me. They had TIME. A whole life for one seam. That is what drowned, if you ask me. Not the cities. The time."

topics.label: Ask what they would make last
lines: "Everyone thinks a masterwork. A crown, a blade, something with a name." Odar Flameforge shakes their head slowly. "The last thing I make will be a hinge, or a latch, or a pot mend, because somebody will need it that afternoon. And that is right. The craft was never the grand things. It was the settlement working, one small fix at a time, and I would be glad to go out mid-fix."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You reached past a working forge to take from me." Odar's tone does not change. "You are lucky. I am not going to say more than that."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: Silvan gestures at the cloth rather than speaking, then relents. "Relics. I do not name them. Naming a thing is a claim about what it is, and I do not make claims."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "Aetherborn." A pause long enough to be an answer in itself. "We do not have a people. We have a diagnosis. Anyone the flood changed gets the same word, and the word does very little work."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "They are not artefacts." Silvan touches one, briefly. "That is the wrong shape of thought. They are PARTS. Every one of these came out of something larger that is still, somewhere, missing them." A long silence. "I sell them because I would rather they were spread out."

topics.label: Ask what the road has taught them
lines: "That you can leave anything behind except your feet." Silvan the Quiet says it lightly, but it has corners. "People think the road is freedom. The road is a landlord like any other — it takes its rent in soles and weather and names of places you will not see twice. I pay it because I am worse at paying the other kind."

topics.label: Ask about a place that stayed with them
lines: "There is a bend in a river, south, past the third ford, where somebody planted a garden and never came back for it." Silvan the Quiet’s voice settles. "It keeps blooming. Nobody tends it and it blooms anyway, in rows — you can still read the ROWS. I have slept there four times and I have never once picked anything. It would be like interrupting somebody."

topics.label: Ask what would make them stop walking
lines: Silvan the Quiet looks at you the way people look at a question they have been avoiding on purpose. "There was a door once. A whole winter behind it. I fixed their fence, I learned their kettle, I started recognizing the dogs." The pause has weight. "I left in the spring like the road was calling and the truth is nothing called. Staying was TERRIFYING and walking was easy, and I have been telling that story backwards to strangers ever since. You are the first one who got it the right way round."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: Silvan says nothing at all, and goes on saying it, and after a while you understand that this is the entire response and it is not going to end.

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Wilderness kit," Bran says. "Traps, feed, the sort of rope that does not mind being wet. And advice, free, which is that most animals out there want less to do with you than you think."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "Reclaimer, technically. Mostly I just live further out than the rest of them." He scratches a dog behind the ears. "The Guild calls it a posting. It is a house."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "The animals changed faster than we did." Bran says it without drama. "Three generations. That is all it took. I set traps my grandfather designed and they do not work any more, because the things they were designed for have learned. We have not learned anything since the water."

topics.label: Ask if anything out there is worth finding

lead.hint: There is a collapsed feed-store two days east — the roof went in but the floor held, and nobody has bothered because it looks like nothing

lines: Bran thinks about it properly, which takes a while. "East. Two days, maybe less if you push. There was a feed-store out that way and the roof went in on it." He scratches the dog. "Everyone who passes it sees a hole in the ground. The floor held. Whatever went down with it is still under there and dry."

topics.label: Ask about the dogs
lines: "Strays, the lot of them. Or were." The nearest one thumps its tail at Bran's voice without opening its eyes. "People think I collect them soft-heartedly. It is a working arrangement — nothing on four legs crosses my fence line unannounced, and in exchange nobody here goes hungry or gets left out in the weather." He scratches an ear. "Same deal I would take, honestly."

topics.label: Ask for the advice that is not free
lines: "That one costs a coin, and here it is: when something out there stands its ground instead of running, LOOK BEHIND YOU." Bran holds up a finger. "Standing ground is a message to something else, nine times in ten. You are not the conversation. You are in the middle of it." He pockets the coin you did not remember agreeing to. "Cheap at the price. That one has kept me alive four times that I know of."

topics.label: Ask about living out there
lines: "Quiet, which is not the same as silent." Bran thinks about it the way he thinks about everything, fully. "A settlement is noise with no information in it. Out at mine, every sound is a sentence — what is moving, how big, whether it minds being heard." He nods at the dozing dogs. "They read it all night so I can sleep. Then at dawn they tell me the headlines. Best neighbours I ever had."

topics.label: Ask which animal changed most
lines: "The wasps." Not the answer you expected, and Bran knows it. "Everyone says the big things — the boars, the hounds. But the mud wasps went from a nuisance to an ARCHITECTURE in my lifetime. Paper cities in the dead trees, galleried, vented, defended in shifts." He shakes his head slowly. "My grandfather smoked them out of fence posts. I negotiate with them. I am not joking about the negotiating."

topics.label: Ask what the dogs made of your gift
lines: "Funny thing about that." Bran nods at the grey-muzzled one by the door. "She does not let anyone's things stay on my table — carries them to the boundary rock, her rules, always has. Your gift has been on that table since you gave it." He looks at you with plain, unhurried interest. "I trust her arithmetic over mine. She counts you as household now. That is not a thing I can undo, so mind you keep deserving it."

topics.label: Ask who the second chair is for
lines: Bran looks at the chair like it might answer for him. "Tamsin. My wife — still is, as far as either of us has said out loud." He fills the kettle, for something to do. "She lasted eleven years out here. It was not the quiet that beat her, it was the winters of it. She lives at the settlement now, keeps the infirmary garden." A slow breath. "We trade letters through Felra's stall and she visits when the road is dry. Some things do not break. They just... live at different distances. The chair stays."

topics.label: Ask why he feeds strays
lines: "Because I was one." Bran says it without ceremony. "After the water took my family's stead I was nine, and I was fed by a woman at a fence line who never once asked my name or my story. Fed me a whole winter. She said feeding a stray is a bet the world places on itself." He sets down the bowl he has been holding. "I have been paying her bet forward for forty years. Dogs, mostly. People, twice." He glances up. "Three times, maybe. We will see how you turn out."

topics.label: Ask what the learning means
lines: "You remember what I said — three generations and my grandfather's traps stopped working." Bran stares into the fire a while. "Here is the part that keeps me up. Learning that fast is not natural selection, it is TEACHING. Something is passing it along." The grey-muzzled dog lifts her head, reading his voice. "I watched a boar sow walk her young around one of my snares last spring. Around it. In order. Like a lesson." He scratches the dog until she settles. "We are not the only ones raising our children carefully any more. I have not decided how to feel about that."

topics.label: Ask where he stopped setting traps

lead.hint: The den valley north of Bran's stead — he pulled every trap out three seasons ago because what is denning there now keeps the whole valley's peace, and something under the old warren glints metal at dusk

lines: "There is a valley north of my stead I pulled every trap out of, three seasons back." Bran refills your cup before he goes on, which is how he buys thinking time. "Something dens there now that keeps ORDER. No kills inside the valley — anywhere. The boars water beside the hounds, and everything walks in slow." He turns the cup in his hands. "And under the old warren mouth, at dusk, something glints. Metal. Worked metal, down a den no digger made." He meets your eye. "I will not disturb the peace of that valley on curiosity. But you go places I do not. Walk in slow, mind, or do not walk in."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You took from a man who feeds strays." Bran looks more disappointed than angry. "That is a low thing. Go on."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Close work," Vela says, laying out a gauntlet. "Armour for people who intend to be within arm's reach. It is heavier and it is honest."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "Tartarian, same as Irma, different valley." She catches your look. "Yes, there are valleys. Everyone thinks we came from one place. There were nine, and seven of them are under the mud."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "I make armour for a fight I do not believe in." Vela sets the gauntlet down. "Every faction on this map is arming for the others and none of them are arming for the WATER, which is the only thing that has ever actually beaten us. I make the plate anyway. That is my part in it."

topics.label: Ask what the work is really like
lines: "Waiting," Vela Ironheart says flatly. "Nine parts waiting, one part everything at once. The stories keep the one part and sell it as the whole trade." A shrug. "Nobody sings about standing in the rain outside a door. The rain is the job."

topics.label: Ask if there is work they will not take
lines: "Three things." Vela Ironheart counts them plainly, a recitation worn smooth. "Nothing against children. Nothing against someone already down. And nothing where the coin is too good for the story I am being told — overpay is the surest sign the story is missing its worst part."

topics.label: Ask what keeps them up at night
lines: "Not the ones I have fought. The one I walked away from." Vela Ironheart looks at the middle distance. "There was a job I turned down for good reasons, and somebody hungrier took it, and it went the way I knew it would. You can be right and still owe. That is the ledger nobody teaches you to keep."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You will not be sold to here again," Vela says. "Not because of the value. Because I put armour on people's bodies, and I have to be able to look at them."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Earth-gear," Mara says. "Anything that holds when the ground does not. Half of Tartaria is standing on something that has already decided to move."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "Golem-kin. Not built — born, whatever the stories say." A dry look. "The stories are better. I have stopped correcting them."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "I can feel it under the settlements." Mara puts a palm flat on the table. "There is a rhythm down there and it is not water. It is too regular for water. I have said this to four people in my life and three of them stopped speaking to me."

topics.label: Ask which scar taught the most
lines: Mara Stoneskin considers the question like an opponent. "This one." Not the biggest — a thin line along the forearm. "First season. I blocked with the edge, like a fool, because holding the blade felt safer than holding the distance. The distance is the weapon. Everything after that scar has been footwork."

topics.label: Ask who taught them the trade
lines: Mara Stoneskin is quiet a moment. "Somebody better than me who did not live to see it. That is the honest answer for anyone in this work, and the ones who claim otherwise trained alone." They check a strap that did not need checking. "You carry your teacher in your guard. Mine is still keeping my left side honest."

topics.label: Ask what comes after the blade
lines: Mara Stoneskin does not laugh at the question, which tells you something. "A door I can bar from the inside. Somewhere the weather is the loudest thing that happens." A pause. "Everyone in this trade has the same dream and none of us can sit still in a quiet room for an hour. I have tried. I lasted forty minutes and checked the door twice."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "Take, then." Mara does not rise. "The ground under this stall remembers weight. So do I."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Wind-gear," says Yara. "Cloaks that do not fight the air, masks for the dust seasons. Everyone prepares for the mud. The mud is the slow part."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "Aetherborn, and yes I hear it in the air, and no it is not a gift." She adjusts a hanging cloth. "It is a sound that does not stop. You would call it a symptom."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "The wind changed direction eleven years ago and never changed back." Yara says it like a confession. "I have asked everyone who would listen. They say weather. It is not weather. Weather returns."

topics.label: Ask what they are looking for
lines: "The same thing as everyone in my line — the piece that makes the rest make sense." Yara the Windcaller smiles at their own phrasing. "You imagine it as a door, when you start. A vault, a tablet, one big answer. Twenty years in, you understand it is a THREAD. You do not find it. You notice you have been holding it a while."

topics.label: Ask about the strangest thing they have found
lines: Yara the Windcaller weighs how much to say. "A room that had been counted. Every object numbered, in a hand nobody can date — not catalogued, COUNTED, the way you count what you are afraid of losing." They look at you. "Whoever numbered that room knew the water was coming. That is not in any record. The counting IS the record."

topics.label: Ask what finding it would mean
lines: Yara the Windcaller goes quiet in a new way. "You have put your finger on the thing. I have built a whole life out of the looking — the looking is my trade, my mornings, my reason." A slow breath. "If I found it tomorrow, I would be a person who HAS a thing instead of a person who SEEKS a thing, and I do not know that man. Some nights I suspect I walk slower on purpose."

topics.label: Try to say something
lines: "You reached into my stall." Yara turns away. "The air told me before I looked. It always does. That is the part you should find unsettling."

topics.label: Ask about their trade
lines: "Exotic," Zorin says, with a showman's flourish. "Which means I cannot tell you what most of these were for, and I have decided to charge extra for the mystery."

topics.label: Ask about their people
lines: "I come from nobody in particular." He grins. "The Unknowing Masses, they call us, which is a magnificent name for people who simply were not invited to any of the meetings."

topics.label: Ask what they really think
lines: "I sell wonder because I ran out of it." Zorin's patter drops away entirely. "I have handled every strange thing that came through three settlements. Not one of them turned out to be magic. All of them turned out to be MADE. By somebody. Who is not here."

topics.label: Ask what the work is really like
lines: "Waiting," Zorin Nightblade says flatly. "Nine parts waiting, one part everything at once. The stories keep the one part and sell it as the whole trade." A shrug. "Nobody sings about standing in the rain outside a door. The rain is the job."
